messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Mariana Flores was twenty-three when the accident happened at the chemical plant where she worked summers between semesters at community college. She had taken the job to help pay tuition, telling herself it was temporary, just three months of good pay. Her parents had emigrated from Guatemala; her mother worked in housekeeping, her father in construction, and Mariana was the first in her family to pursue a four-year degree. The facility processed industrial solvents, and she had been assigned to the quality control lab—a windowless room on the ground floor where she tested samples and logged results. She had been there for six weeks when the rupture occurred in the storage tank two floors above. She did not see it happen. What she felt first was the acrid smell, sharp and suffocating, flooding through the ventilation system. Then the alarm. Then the evacuation, people moving fast, someone shouting that there was a chemical release, and Mariana running down the corridor with her hand over her mouth, her eyes burning, her throat closing. She made it outside and collapsed on the grass with twenty other workers, gasping, vomiting, her lungs on fire. The ambulance came. The hospital came. The fluorescent lights and the smell of antiseptic and the IV in her arm and the doctor saying she had inhaled enough of the solvent to cause chemical pneumonitis but that she would recover.

She did recover, in the medical sense. The inflammation in her lungs subsided. The burning in her eyes faded. By early autumn, the physical wounds had healed. But something else had not. Now twenty-six, three years after the exposure, Mariana had come to understand her body as something that could betray her without warning. The plant had settled the case quietly; she had received a check and used it to finish her degree. She was now a junior majoring in environmental science, a choice that felt both logical and ironic—she wanted to understand what had happened to her, wanted to prevent it from happening to others. But her body had not moved on. Her body was still in that corridor, still inhaling poison, still convinced that danger was imminent and invisible.

The darkness was the worst. Since the accident, Mariana could not sleep with the lights off. She kept her bedroom lamp on every night, and when she woke in the dark—which happened often—panic seized her before her mind caught up. Her heart would race, her breathing would shallow, and she would lie still, scanning the room for threats she could not name. The hospital smell was nearly as bad. Whenever she caught that antiseptic scent—in a clinic, in a pharmacy, even in someone's home after they had cleaned—her body would tense, her muscles would coil, and she would feel the burning in her lungs return, phantom pain so vivid that she would have to leave the space and breathe outside air until the sensation faded. She had stopped going to the industrial district of the city where the plant was located. She took a longer route to campus to avoid the neighborhood entirely, adding forty minutes to her commute. She could not articulate why—not really. When her roommate asked, Mariana could only say that she did not want to go there, and the roommate had stopped asking. What Mariana could not explain, even to herself, was that she was afraid of what her body would do if she drove past that building. She did not trust it anymore. When someone touched her unexpectedly—her roommate putting a hand on her shoulder, a classmate brushing past her in the library—she would flinch violently, her nervous system firing as if under attack. She had apologized so many times that people had begun to give her space, and that was easier than trying to explain. In her environmental science courses, she had begun to sit in the back row, away from other students, where she could monitor the room and control access to her body. Her lab partner had requested reassignment after Mariana's repeated startled reactions to routine questions disrupted their work. She had tried to explain to the professor that she was not unstable, just careful, but the words sounded hollow even to her own ears.

The memories themselves were fragmented and strange. She knew what had happened—she could recite the facts, the timeline, the aftermath. But she had come to dread the memory itself, and over the months she had developed a kind of private ritual to keep it at bay. When the memory surfaced unbidden, she would deliberately distract herself—turning up music, scrolling through her phone, forcing her attention onto her coursework with an intensity that bordered on desperate. She had even tried writing the event down once, thinking that putting it into words might contain it, but reading back what she had written made the panic worse, made the phantom burning return to her chest and throat. So she had stopped writing. She had stopped talking about it except in the barest terms. She had learned that the less she rehearsed the narrative, the less vivid it became in her waking hours, though it returned with full force in her sleep. When she tried to tell someone what had happened, the words would not come. She would open her mouth and find only silence, or worse, she would start to speak and realize that the sequence in her mind did not match the order in which things actually occurred. The smell, the alarm, the running—or was it the running, then the alarm, then the smell? The confusion frustrated her, made her feel stupid, made her wonder if something was fundamentally wrong with her, if her mind had been damaged along with her lungs. Sometimes, when the memory surfaced unbidden, she would feel pain in her chest and throat, the exact places where the chemical had burned her, even though the doctors had said those tissues were healed. She had also begun to have nightmares in which she was back in the corridor, but this time the doors would not open, and the smell grew thicker and thicker until she woke gasping, her sheets soaked through with sweat, her heart hammering against her ribs.

She had come to believe that there was something defective in her, something broken that could not be fixed. Her body was no longer hers to trust. It reacted to threats that were not there, kept her vigilant in a way that exhausted her, made her startle at shadows and scents. She was constantly tense, constantly scanning, constantly afraid. Her grades, which had always been strong, had begun to slip as her concentration fractured under the weight of hypervigilance. After three years of this, after dropping two classes last semester because she could not concentrate, after watching her friendships narrow as people grew tired of her unpredictability, after her mother called her from Guatemala and heard only flatness in her daughter's voice and wept quietly on the other end of the line, Mariana had finally called the university counseling center. She needed to understand why her body would not let her move forward, why it insisted on keeping her trapped in a moment that was long past. She was hoping that someone could help her find her way back to herself, or at least help her understand the person she had become. What frightened her most was that the strategies she had developed to survive—the avoidance, the suppression, the hypervigilance—had become a prison of their own, one that was slowly collapsing the life she had tried to build. She was also terrified that if she stopped avoiding the memory, if she stopped running from it, the panic would consume her entirely and she would not come back.
